title: Bangalore Watch Company’s First Pocket Watch Looks Back to 1947
description: Inspired by the pivotal year of 1947, Bangalore Watch Company’s first-ever pocket watch combines mid-century design cues with a contemporary take on modern Indian history.
content: Bangalore Watch Company’s First Pocket Watch Looks Back to 1947 A pocket watch inspired by the beginning of modern India Pocket watches are a timeless classic for horological enthusiasts, but they are having a moment. The recent Swatch x Audemars Piguet Royal Oak pocket watch caused quite a stir in the watch world, bringing the traditional format back into the spotlight. Now Bangalore Watch Company is taking its own approach with the Forty-Seven, a pocket watch inspired by the formative years of modern India. Looking back to 1947 The Bangalore Watch Company has built its collections around stories from contemporary India, drawing on subjects including aviation, cricket, space exploration and the outdoors. The Forty-Seven takes a different perspective by going back to the starting point of that narrative. The period following independence was marked by ambitious efforts to build the foundations of a modern nation. At the time, India faced very different economic and social circumstances from those of today. The brand points to a literacy rate of around 12 percent, a per-capita income of approximately $50 and a country carrying significant debt. The decades that followed would see India develop into one of the world's largest and fastest-growing economies. That transformation is the historical backdrop for the Forty-Seven. Rather than celebrating the past for its own sake, Bangalore Watch Company says the timepiece is intended as a tribute to the generation that chose to focus on building the future. “Forty-Seven is a tribute to the years that shaped modern India. A pocket watch was the natural choice, because it belonged to that time,” says Nirupesh Joshi, co-founder of Bangalore Watch Company. “With this watch, the brand goes back to where those stories first began.” A Traditional Pocket-Watch Silhouette The 46mm case follows the proportions and design language of pocket watches from the first half of the 20th century. It is made from 316L surgical steel and finished with rose-gold PVD, giving it a warm appearance. The off-white dial has a linen-like texture and remains deliberately restrained, with the subsidiary seconds at 6 o'clock. The distinctive Arabic numerals, cathedral-style hour hand, and minute hand are coated with Swiss Superluminova, ensuring clear legibility even in the dark. The dial is protected by a K1 hardened crystal. A push-and-pull crown bearing the Bangalore Watch Company logo sits at the top of the case, while the closed case back can be personalized with an engraving, giving owners the option to add a personal message or inscription. Quartz Rather Than Nostalgia Inside, Forty-Seven uses a Swiss-made Ronda 6004.D quartz movement. It provides the straightforward three-hand display expected of a pocket watch and offers a battery life of approximately 40 months. The choice of quartz is notable in a product so closely tied to traditional watchmaking. Bangalore Watch Company has previously emphasized technical experimentation across its collections, including the use of recovered aircraft and aircraft-carrier materials, meteorites and captured carbon. With the Forty-Seven, the focus is less on mechanical complexity than on the object itself and the story it represents. Leather Lanyard and Rose-Gold Clip The traditional pocket-watch character continues with the attachment. The Forty-Seven comes with a lanyard-style genuine leather strap described by the brand as oil-pulled leather. A matching rose-gold-colored clip completes the ensemble and allows the watch to be carried in a pocket or attached to clothing. The Bangalore Watch Company Forty-Seven is priced at $1,250. (Discover more timepieces designed to be worn beyond the wrist.)

title: In a Farewell to Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer Launches Formula 1 Solargraph
description: For the final Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer introduces two limited-edition Formula 1 Solargraph models in a compact 38mm format.
content: In a Farewell to Circuit Zandvoort, TAG Heuer Launches Formula 1 Solargraph Special edition of two limited series TAG Heuer marks the final Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Circuit Zandvoort, which will take place from 21 to 23 August 2026, with two new Formula 1 Solargraph limited editions. Limited to 1,500 and 1,000 pieces respectively, a distinguish by ones rubber strap and the other's steel bracelet, the watches combine a 38mm sandblasted steel case with a gray opaline dial, orange and red accents, and the Formula 1 collection’s bold design language. Both watches are powered by the brand's light-driven TH50-00 Solargraph movement. The choice of Zandvoort as the inspiration for the two watches reflects the circuit’s place in Formula 1 history and its distinctive setting on the Dutch coast. The track runs through the dunes and features tight sections and banked corners, while Formula 1’s return to the venue has become closely associated with the orange-clad crowds filling the grandstands to support Max Verstappen in a festival-like beachside setting. A Compact Formula 1 Case The two new models bring the Formula 1 collection back to a 38mm case size, echoing the proportions of earlier watches from the line when it was introduced in 1986. The sandblasted steel construction gives the case a matte surface, while the bidirectional TH-Polylight bezel features an orange 60-second/minute scale. A flat sapphire crystal with anti-reflective treatment protects the dial with bright orange and red accents inspired by the visual identity of Zandvoort and its distinctive racing atmosphere. Red lacquered applied indexes and hour and minute hands are filled with eggshell-colored Superluminova, which glows green in the dark. The central seconds hand and TAG Heuer logo are also rendered in red. Both versions feature a date display at 3 o’clock and are water-resistant to 100 meters. Two Versions, One Solargraph Movement The technical platform is the same for both editions, with each opting for the TAG Heuer’s TH50-00 quartz movement, which draws energy from both natural and artificial light. According to the brand, one minute of direct sunlight provides enough energy for approximately one day of operation. A full charge requires less than 40 hours of light exposure and provides up to ten months of autonomy in complete darkness. Should the watch stop, just ten seconds of exposure to light is sufficient to restart it. The accumulator is designed to last for up to 15 years. The first version, the reference WBY111H.FT8128, is limited to 1,500 pieces and comes with an orange rubber strap and steel pin buckle. The second, reference WBY111L.BA0042, is limited to 1,000 pieces and pairs the 38mm case with a three-row sandblasted steel bracelet. Its folding clasp features double safety push-buttons and an adjustment-link extension. Both will be available from this month and will retail for $2,150 and $2,250, respectively.

title: Seven of the Best Alternatives to the Rolex Submariner
description: The Rolex Submariner is the world’s most famous dive watch, but compelling alternatives from Omega, Tudor, TAG Heuer, and others range from accessible to decidedly luxurious.
content: Seven of the Best Alternatives to the Rolex Submariner Seven watches that offer their own take on the modern luxury diver The Rolex Submariner is the archetype of an entire watch category: the dive watch. For decades, it has set the benchmark for design, precision, reliability, durability, and legibility. At the same time, its sporty elegance has carried it far beyond the world of professional diving. Few watches combine brand prestige, desirability, instant recognition, and everyday versatility quite so effortlessly. Yet that very popularity makes the search for alternatives even more interesting. A high-quality dive watch does not have to be a Submariner. Some models come remarkably close in terms of status, specifications, and price. Others take a more individual approach — more technical, more historically driven, more elegant, or considerably more affordable. Our selection therefore ranges from high-end manufacture pieces and accomplished Swiss sports watches to attractive entry-level models with automatic movements and 300 meters of water resistance. The goal was not to find watches that simply look like the Submariner. Instead, we focused on models capable of fulfilling a similar role: robust, versatile, and equally suited to everyday wear, travel, and water. Omega Seamaster Diver 300M The Omega Seamaster Diver 300M is arguably the most prominent alternative to the Rolex Submariner. Since its introduction in 1993, the collection has become one of Omega’s most important sports-watch lines, combining genuine diving capability with a strong presence on the wrist. Its James Bond connection helped make it famous. For anyone seeking a luxury dive watch that combines advanced mechanics, Swiss watchmaking heritage, and a touch of pop culture, the Seamaster makes a compelling case. At 42mm, it is slightly larger than the Submariner, but it likewise offers 300 meters of water resistance and a unidirectional dive bezel. One of its defining differences is the dial, with its distinctive wave pattern, along with the characteristically scalloped bezel that gives the Seamaster Diver 300M an unmistakable visual identity. Omega’s strongest argument, however, may be the movement. The Co-Axial Master Chronometer caliber 8806 is METAS-certified, offers a 55-hour power reserve, and resists magnetic fields up to 15,000 gauss. The Omega is also equipped with a helium escape valve at 10 o’clock, reinforcing its credentials as a professional dive watch. For anyone looking for a high-end diver from a major brand, backed by strong history and a design language entirely its own, the Seamaster Diver 300M remains one of the most convincing alternatives to the Rolex Submariner. Reference 210.30.42.20.01.010 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Omega Co-Axial Master Chronometer caliber 8806, automatic | 55-hour power reserve | Approximately $8,100 Tudor Black Bay 58 The Tudor Black Bay 58 is one of the most obvious alternatives to the Rolex Submariner, because Tudor has not only long-standing historical ties to Rolex but also a distinguished dive-watch heritage of its own. Its name refers to 1958, the year Tudor introduced Ref. 7924, a dive watch water-resistant to 200 meters. That combination of heritage, robust engineering, and wearable proportions is precisely what makes the Black Bay 58 so appealing. At 39mm, it is more compact than many modern sports watches. Its three-link steel bracelet, with distinctive rivet-style detailing, also has a more individual character than Rolex’s familiar Oyster bracelet. Compared with the Submariner, however, the Black Bay is less status-driven. Its design is more understated and carries a subtle retro character, thanks to Tudor’s signature Snowflake hour hand, first introduced in 1969. It is also considerably more accessible in price. Inside is the manufacture caliber MT5400-U. The movement is certified by both COSC and METAS, features a silicon balance spring, and offers a 65-hour power reserve. Reference M7939A1A0NU-0002 | Stainless steel, 39mm | 200 meters of water resistance | Manufacture caliber MT5400-U, automatic | 65-hour power reserve | Approximately $5,600 TAG Heuer Aquaracer Professional 300 Date The TAG Heuer Aquaracer Professional 300 Date is one of the strongest Submariner alternatives in the mid-luxury segment. It delivers nearly everything expected of a modern dive watch: a robust stainless-steel case, 300 meters of water resistance, a screw-down crown, sapphire crystal, ceramic bezel, and a solid steel bracelet with a safety folding clasp. At the same time, it looks markedly more angular and technical than the Rolex, particularly with its 12-sided bezel, blue wave-pattern dial, and orange seconds hand. TAG Heuer has steadily refined the Aquaracer in recent years, and its greatest strength now lies in its specifications. The current Professional 300 Date is powered by the COSC-certified TH31-00 caliber, produced by Sellita’s AMT manufacture division, and offers an impressive 80-hour power reserve. Despite its 42mm diameter, the watch remains comparatively slim at 12mm thick. For anyone seeking a distinctive, robust Swiss dive watch with a chronometer-certified movement, the Aquaracer Professional 300 Date is a particularly compelling and rational alternative. Reference WBP5111.BA0013 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Caliber TH31-00 COSC, automatic, AMT/Sellita | 80-hour power reserve | Approximately $5,200 Longines HydroConquest The Longines HydroConquest is an insider tip for anyone seeking a high-quality Swiss dive watch without stepping into high-end luxury territory. Compared with the Submariner, it feels more contemporary and is considerably more accessible in price. Its unidirectional ceramic bezel, prominently styled minute hand, and excellent legibility in low light and underwater give it the unmistakable character of a purpose-built diver. Water resistance to 300 meters reinforces those credentials. The 39mm version, in particular, combines the robustness of a full-fledged dive watch with compact, contemporary proportions, making it equally suitable for everyday wear, travel, and more active use. Inside is a modern automatic movement produced exclusively for Longines by ETA, its sister company within the Swatch Group. It offers an impressive power reserve of up to 72 hours. For anyone looking for strong value in a Swiss mechanical dive watch, the HydroConquest deserves serious consideration. Reference L3.779.4.56.6 | Stainless steel, 39mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Longines caliber L888.5, automatic | Approximately 72-hour power reserve | Approximately $2,500 Breitling Superocean Heritage B31 Automatic 42 The Breitling Superocean Heritage B31 Automatic 42 is an appealing Submariner alternative for anyone drawn to a major brand with a strong history and a more individual sense of elegance. The model traces its roots to the original Superocean of 1957, a watch conceived not merely as a professional diving instrument, but as a stylish sports watch in its own right. The 42mm stainless-steel model remains a fully capable dive watch, with a unidirectional bezel featuring a ceramic insert, a screw-down crown, and water resistance to 200 meters. Its distinctive character comes from the arrow-shaped hour hand, spear-shaped minute hand, unconventional hour markers, and domed sapphire crystal. Together, these details reflect Breitling’s “modern retro” design philosophy. Power comes from the automatic three-hand caliber B31. The movement is chronometer-certified and delivers approximately 78 hours of power reserve. Reference AB3111241B1A1 | Stainless steel, 42mm | 200 meters of water resistance | Manufacture caliber B31, automatic | COSC-certified chronometer | Approximately 78-hour power reserve | Approximately $7,700 Tissot: Seastar 1000 Powermatic 80 For anyone seeking a particularly affordable dive watch with plenty to offer both technically and visually, Tissot makes a strong case. The Seastar 1000 Powermatic 80 does not pretend to compete with the Rolex Submariner in status or finishing, but it delivers many of the features expected of a modern dive watch. Its 40mm stainless-steel case is fitted with a sapphire crystal, screw-down crown, screw-down caseback, unidirectional bezel, and 300 meters of water resistance. As part of the Swatch Group, Tissot is one of the best-known Swiss brands in the entry-level mechanical segment, and the Seastar benefits from that position. It feels sporty, well made, and thoroughly practical while remaining far more affordable than traditional luxury divers. A black dial, bold hands and markers with Super-LumiNova, and a steel bracelet with a quick-release system make it an easy choice for everyday wear, travel, and time in the water. The movement is another strong point: the Powermatic 80 delivers up to 80 hours of power reserve and features an antimagnetic Nivachron hairspring. Reference T120.807.11.051.00 | Stainless steel, 40mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Powermatic 80, automatic, based on ETA C.07 | Up to 80-hour power reserve | Approximately $900 Glashütte Original SeaQ Panorama Date The Glashütte Original SeaQ Panorama Date is one of the most compelling alternatives to the Rolex Submariner for buyers who value not only dive-watch capability, but also manufacture pedigree and a distinct sense of origin. Part of Glashütte Original’s Spezialist collection, the SeaQ traces its lineage to the Spezimatic Type RP TS 200 of 1969, giving it a genuine German dive-watch heritage of its own. Its 43.2mm stainless-steel case, unidirectional ceramic bezel, screw-down crown, sapphire crystal, and 300 meters of water resistance meet the essential requirements of a professional dive watch. Compared with the Submariner, the SeaQ is larger and more assertive on the wrist. It also adds a useful and visually distinctive complication: the brand’s Panorama Date at 4 o’clock. Inside is the manufacture caliber 36-13. Its architecture includes the traditional Glashütte three-quarter plate, while technical features include a 100-hour power reserve and a silicon balance spring. Finishing is equally elaborate, with beveled edges, Glashütte ribbing, and a skeletonized rotor fitted with a 21-karat gold oscillating weight. For anyone looking for a luxury dive watch with strong brand identity, serious technical substance, and unmistakable German manufacture character, the SeaQ Panorama Date is a particularly distinctive alternative to the Submariner. Reference 1-36-13-01-80-70 | Stainless steel, 43.2mm | 300 meters of water resistance | Manufacture caliber 36-13, automatic | 100-hour power reserve | Approximately $15,600

title: Introducing the Seiko Presage Classic Series Tradman’s Bonsai
description: Seiko draws on the Japanese art of bonsai for a new Presage Classic Series limited edition, pairing a textured deep-green dial with warm gold-colored details and a self-winding movement with a 72-hour power reserve.
content: Introducing the Seiko Presage Classic Series Tradman’s Bonsai Inspired by the Japanese black pine Since its introduction in 2016, the Seiko Presage collection has explored Japanese craftsmanship and design traditions through mechanical watches. The latest addition to the Presage Classic Series takes its inspiration from an especially enduring element of Japanese culture: bonsai. The Presage Classic Series Tradman’s Bonsai Limited Edition HCC009J1 translates the appearance of a Japanese black pine into a refined wristwatch with a deep-green dial, gold-colored accents, and a compact 38mm case. A Black Pine as Inspiration For the new limited edition, Seiko collaborated with Tradman’s Bonsai, a Japanese collective that brings together traditional bonsai cultivation with contemporary design, fashion, and art. The starting point for the watch was a black pine viewed in moonlight, with its characteristic needles providing the inspiration for the dial color. Known as Matsuba-iro, the deep green is associated in Japan with good fortune and prosperity. Its subtly textured surface evokes the bark of the tree, while also creating gentle variations in the way light is reflected across the dial. The effect is deliberately restrained. Gold-colored hands and applied indexes stand out against the dark green background, while the absence of a date display keeps the composition clean. The result is a classic combination of colors that gives the watch a decidedly elegant character. A Classic Presage with Refined Proportions The HCC009J1 measures 38mm in diameter and 12.9mm in thickness. Its compact case features a gold-colored finish and a finely knurled bezel, adding another layer of texture to the design. A sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating on both sides protects the dial. Despite its dressier appearance, the watch retains the practical character expected from the Presage Classic Series, with water resistance to 100 meters. The Japanese watch is delivered on a seven-row metal bracelet and comes with an additional leather strap. The latter features a Sanko-matsu pattern inspired by the needles of the pine tree. The traditional Japanese motif is also associated with good fortune, extending the bonsai theme beyond the dial. Automatic Movement with Three Days of Power Behind the exhibition case back, Seiko's automatic Caliber 6R51 provides the mechanical drive. The movement offers more than 72 hours of power reserve, allowing the watch to run for roughly three days when fully wound. The movement incorporates Seiko's Magic Lever winding system and a stop-seconds function, enabling the wearer to halt the seconds hand when setting the time. Through the transparent case back, the movement becomes an additional element of the watch's mechanical character. The Seiko Presage Classic Series Tradman’s Bonsai Limited Edition HCC009J1 is limited to 2,000 pieces worldwide. It will be available from September 2026 for $1,350.

title: Perrelet and IFL Watches Turn the Weekend GMT into a Hand-Painted Travelogue
description: Perrelet and Dubai-based IFL Watches transform the Weekend GMT into a 50-piece tribute to travel, with individually hand-painted dials, a second-time-zone display, and the in-house caliber P-401.
content: Perrelet and IFL Watches Turn the Weekend GMT into a Hand-Painted Travelogue Fifty hand-painted dials, each with its own itinerary Perrelet has teamed up with Dubai-based dial specialist IFL Watches to introduce a new artistic interpretation of its Weekend GMT. Limited to just 50 pieces, the Weekend GMT Atlas combines the Swiss brand's in-house mechanics with IFL Watches' signature hand-painted miniature artwork, transforming each dial into a unique expression of travel and discovery. A Different Journey on Every Dial The defining feature is the individually hand-painted dial, which turns each watch into a miniature work of art. At the center is a compass rose, long regarded as a symbol of navigation, while the surrounding landscape brings together scenes inspired by destinations around the world. Dolphins leap through turquoise waters, lush tropical vegetation frames the composition, and the pyramids of Egypt complete the colorful panorama. Since every dial is painted by hand, no two watches are exactly alike. The artwork is seamlessly integrated with the watch’s GMT function. A satin-finished blue 24-hour ring surrounds the central compass motif, allowing the dedicated GMT hand, with its white, red-outlined triangular tip, to display home time at a glance. Applied rhodium-plated baton markers maintain strong legibility without distracting from the artwork, while a discreet date window at 3 o’clock rounds out the practical, travel-oriented layout. Compact Dimensions for Everyday Wear The Weekend GMT Atlas retains the understated proportions of the collection introduced in 2019. Its stainless-steel case measures 39mm in diameter and just 9.61mm thick, combining brushed and polished finishes for a versatile appearance that works equally well in casual and more formal settings. Offering 50 meters of water resistance, the watch comes fitted with a seven-row stainless-steel bracelet featuring alternating satin-brushed and polished surfaces. Perrelet also includes a blue leather strap with an alligator pattern, and both can be exchanged quickly through an integrated, tool-free quick-release system. An In-House Automatic GMT Movement Inside the case beats Perrelet’s in-house automatic caliber P-401, developed by sister company Soprod. Operating at 4 Hz, or 28,800 vibrations per hour, the movement delivers a 42-hour power reserve and features 25 jewels. Local time is displayed by the central hour and minute hands, while the independently adjustable GMT hand tracks a second time zone on the 24-hour scale, making the watch well suited to frequent travelers. The movement is visible through a mineral-glass porthole in the screw-down caseback, which also carries a decorative engraving echoing the dial artwork and the individual limited-edition number. Visible finishing includes circular-grained bridges and an openworked, rhodium-plated oscillating weight bearing the Perrelet logo. Pricing and Availability The Perrelet x IFL Watches Weekend GMT Atlas is limited to 50 pieces and available now through IFL Watches, authorized Perrelet retailers, and the brand’s online store. It is priced at $3,450.

title: Traveling Along the Horological Silk Road Between Switzerland and China
description: Outsourcing has long been a part of Swiss watchmaking, but in recent years, China’s role as a manufacturing partner has grown in both scale and quality. This evolving relationship is reshaping not only the global supply chain, but also the development of China’s own high-end watch industry.
content: Traveling Along the Horological Silk Road Between Switzerland and China How outsourcing the production of components for Swiss watch brands has influenced China’s own watch industry It is often said that the best brand that the Swiss ever created was for themselves. As a result, the label “Swiss Made” has become much more than a country-of-origin indication and is regarded worldwide both as a seal of approval and a guarantee for outstanding quality, especially in the world of watches. Needless to say, while clever marketing certainly has played a role in making this stick in the minds of generations of watch enthusiasts, this achievement would not have been possible without decades of producing watches worthy of their reputation for being exceptional in quality. This makes the Swiss-made label extremely valuable, in fact, so valuable that the Swiss government created a law more than 50 years ago to regulate and protect the use of it. (Various studies, in particular those carried out by the ETH Zurich and the University of St. Gallen, have shown that consumers are generally prepared to pay up to 20-percent more for a Swiss watch, and even up to 50-percent more for mechanical pieces.) According to the most recent “Ordinance for Watches” that came into force in 2017, a watch is considered Swiss if, at least, the mechanical construction and prototyping of the watch have been carried out in Switzerland (and for watches that are not exclusively mechanical, this also includes the design of the printed circuits, the display, and the software). Further requirements are that at least 60 percent of the manufacturing costs are incurred in Switzerland, that its movement is Swiss and cased up in Switzerland, and that the final inspection of the watch is conducted by the manufacturer in Switzerland. For a movement to earn the Swiss-made label, it also needs to meet all of the above, with the addition that it needs to contain parts made in Switzerland, excluding the cost of assembling them, that represent at least 50 percent of the value of all the constituent parts. Despite these efforts, spearheaded by the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry (FH), to strengthen the definition of Swiss made, this also means that, like Swiss cheese, some (loop)holes still allow brands to rely on producers outside of Switzerland and create a Swiss-made product. Obviously, just because there is an option to have components produced outside of Switzerland and still have the words “Swiss Made” on the dial, doesn’t mean that a brand has to take advantage of that. More importantly, it doesn’t automatically mean customers are cheated when it does so: The reputation of Italian leather, for example, is about as good as that of Swiss chocolate (which, while we’re at it, contains beans that are most often sourced from Africa and South America). Also, the typical watch buyer usually doesn’t insist on locally produced packaging to go with it, and a highly skilled independent watchmaker might suddenly be more adept when it comes to the injection-molding of parts required for rubber straps. Which means that, ultimately, the decision to outsource very much depends on a brand’s production capabilities and (desired) performance in the market, both in terms of pricing as well as perception. And it works both ways: In 1868, Bostonian watchmaker Florentine Ariosto Jones certainly didn’t pick Schaffhausen to build a watch factory solely because of the famous Hallstatt-style rowing village nearby. Keeping Swiss Made Accessible Especially for a brand aiming to sell high volumes of mid-priced or mid-luxury products, relying on a supplier outside a high-wage country like Switzerland can make much more sense than an exclusive brand that is, for example, all about handmade finishing and complicated movements. That means that producing specific components outside of Switzerland can allow a brand to make watches at a more competitive price point, while maintaining or even increasing profitability — quite often thanks to suppliers that are based in China. While a majority of brands generally don’t disclose where individual parts of their watches are made, even when it is in the same country, be it for strategic or image-related reasons, at least one brand is so open about it that it puts this info on the watch. Quite often, models of the Zurich-based watch brand SevenFriday feature a caseback with a small map that tells you that the concept and design of the watch were created in Switzerland, and the movement came from Japan, and everything else was made in China. In a conversation about this topic with Dan Niederer, founder and CEO of SevenFriday, Niederer mentioned that this openly global approach to the production of his watches happened naturally when he founded the brand in 2012. He and his entire team later built on the Swiss way of working with SevenFriday, where ideas move to make frequent changes early in the market that still often benefit from being in every way “Made in Switzerland” from the beginning. The stories of Chinese watch brands often begin the same way as the launch of any other watch brand: a deep passion for mechanical watchmaking. Even if you have been testing them regularly, they still consider it to be a bit costly. As the movement is a vital piece of a mechanical watch for obvious reasons, he is looking for the best options at the targeted price point. In his opinion, these can currently be found in Japan, resulting in the majority of SevenFriday models being powered by automatic movements made by Miyota, an integrated manufacturer of movements that belongs to Citizen Watch Co., Ltd. While the Chinese calibers are not yet on the same level in this category, Niederer explained that the Chinese are very good at production processes. Needless to say, other Swiss companies have also noticed this and some have even set up facilities to produce parts in China at a lower cost, which has, in turn, accelerated the knowledge transfer in both directions. From Original Equipment Manufacturer to Creating a Brand More importantly, the Chinese watch brands themselves have become much more active and successful in the global luxury watch market. In 2021, CIGA Design won the Challenge Watch prize at the prestigious Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) with its ‘Blue Planet,’ making it the first Chinese brand ever to do so, and most likely it won’t be the last. Another brand that is making serious strides this way is Behrens. It was founded in 2012 in Shenzhen, a vibrant manufacturing city and special economic zone on the east bank of the Pearl River estuary on the central coast of the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, bordering Hong Kong to the south. Behrens aims to create innovative movements without any operating complications. The driving force behind Behrens is Lin Bingguang, and his story is not that different from any other entrepreneur who decides to start a watch brand. He was fascinated by mechanical clocks and watches at a young age, and as he grew older, he wanted to share his passion for timepieces with the world. When asked what advantages he sees for Chinese watchmaking compared to other parts of the world, Bingguang starts with a shortcoming: He’s seen for a long time that Chinese-made watches give the impression of lacking original design and advanced watchmaking technology. He aims to offer Chinese originality and high quality through his own brand, making the industry in his home country put, in his feel, the value of creativity. He also points out that, in his opinion, China, as the world’s largest production center, has undergone apparent changes in recent years, transitioning its manufacturing industry from labor-intensive to technology-intensive. This is ideal for a brand like Behrens because it not only means that quality parts are becoming available more easily, but also that more complex designs can become a reality. In terms of competition, Bingguang is also looking toward a vibrant market. He sees that the challenges Behrens faces in the market are not caused by the established watch companies, but rather by the accessibility of Swiss watchmaking. He considers the entire Swiss and European watchmaking industry worthy of learning from in terms of building a brand and product, from materials to marketing. And it’s not just the most established high-volume manufacturers like Fiyta, Rossini, Tian Wang, Sea-Gull, Bohlly, Starking and Golgen that have become more refined over the years: Hong Kong-based Atelier Wen was founded in 2018 by Robin Tallendier and Wilfried Buiron, whose initial goal is creating a “high quality experience with a Chinese soul.” This also indicates what the Red Dragon’s watch industry can offer the whole world, beyond being a capable producer of competently produced components. Based on the character and culture of the country, Chinese watch manufacturers can add a unique flavor to a brand that is often difficult to emulate. This expertise, perfected by decades of experience in the watchmaking industry, will eventually benefit from increasing production quality — something that could shift perceptions both in China and globally. This article was originally published in the March / April 2024 print issue of WatchTime Magazine. To subscribe to the Magazine, click here.

title: Voici les chaussures Type R pour devenir le plus cool de la cour de récré
description: La Honda Civic Type R devient accessible aux plus jeunes, mais pas exactement comme ils l’espéraient. Honda et Achilles ont transformé l’univers de la sportive japonaise en une paire de baskets pour enfants vendue environ 41 dollars. Logos, couleurs et détails sportifs sont de la partie, les 325 ch nettement moins.
content: Voici les chaussures Type R pour devenir le plus cool de la cour de récré La Honda Civic Type R devient accessible aux plus jeunes, mais pas exactement comme ils l’espéraient. Honda et Achilles ont transformé l’univers de la sportive japonaise en une paire de baskets pour enfants vendue environ 41 dollars. Logos, couleurs et détails sportifs sont de la partie, les 325 ch nettement moins. Disposer du blason sportif Type R est devenu plus accessible. Beaucoup plus accessible. Pour 6 490 yens (35 euros environ au cours actuel), inutile toutefois d’espérer repartir avec les 325 ch de la Civic : cette version se porte aux pieds et fonctionne exclusivement à l’énergie humaine. Honda s’est associé à la marque japonaise Achilles pour créer des baskets insolites destinées aux enfants. Comme leur nom le présage, ces dernières s’inspirent de la compacte musclée. Basées sur les Syunsoku Ultima Cheetah, elles poussent le mimétisme assez loin : logo Type R sur l’avant, emblème Honda rouge au talon et surpiqûres contrastées rappelant l’habitacle. Trois teintes sont proposées. Les amateurs auront à choisir entre Championship White, Frame Red et Racing Blue Pearl. Même la technique tente de jouer au sport automobile avec des éléments spécifiques. Semelle asymétrique pour améliorer l’adhérence en virage, construction légère et système « Inner Flex » doivent aider les jeunes pilotes à négocier la cour de récréation avec davantage de conviction. Pas pour les adultes Disponibles de la pointure 25 à 36, ces chaussures sont livrées dans une boîte décorée d’une belle Civic Type R. Les précommandes sont ouvertes au Japon jusqu’au 27 septembre avec des livraisons prévues début octobre. Reste à vérifier le chrono sur un tour de préau.

title: The Watch Came First: Inside Louis Vuitton and Singer’s Porsche 911 Collaboration
description: Louis Vuitton’s first full automotive collaboration with Singer began with a mechanical dashboard clock and grew into two bespoke Porsche 911s with matching watches and accessories.
content: The Watch Came First: Inside Louis Vuitton and Singer’s Porsche 911 Collaboration A dashboard clock became two one-off Porsche 911s Every great collaboration has an origin story, and this one begins somewhere unexpected: not on a runway, not in a design studio, but on the dashboard of a car. Louis Vuitton's watch division, La Fabrique du Temps, was asked to build a single dashboard clock for a customized Porsche. One clock turned into two full vehicles, a year-long partnership, and Louis Vuitton's first-ever complete automotive project — done in collaboration with Singer, the California-based atelier whose restorations of classic Porsche 911s have made it something of a cult name among collectors. The result: two reimagined Porsche 911s, built on the beloved 964 chassis, each one a rolling argument for what happens when a luxury maison's savoir-faire meets a car culture obsessed with precision. Two Cars, Two Distinct Personalities The first, simply called the Classic, is a coupé finished in saffron and cobalt blue — colors pulled straight from Louis Vuitton's archives, with a lineage that traces back over 150 years to a 1924 trunk made for Citroën. Under the hood: a naturally aspirated 4.0-liter flat-six, a six-speed manual, and carbon-ceramic brakes. The second, the Classic Turbo, is a cabriolet developed under the direction of Nicolas Ghesquière, Louis Vuitton's Artistic Director of Women's Collections. Painted in Calcaire Lutétien white and finished with wood trim inside, it trades motorsport bravado for something closer to the elegance of a vintage motorboat. A 3.8-liter twin-turbo flat-six with selectable drive modes sits underneath all that restraint. The Clock That Started It All Here's where things get genuinely interesting for anyone who loves objects with mechanisms inside them: both cars carry a fully functional, hand-wound clock on the dashboard — not a design flourish, an actual mechanical instrument. Each one runs on an eight-day power reserve, ticks at 18,000 vibrations per hour, and carries the engraved double signature "Louis Vuitton Paris, Fab. En Suisse." Pop it out of its housing, set it on its included stand, and it becomes a desk clock. It's the kind of detail that rewards the kind of person who'd actually notice it. On the Classic, the clock sits to the right of the dashboard, framed by four Tambour-inspired gauges. On the Classic Turbo, it's mounted front and center in the console, with gold-toned dials and five gauges total — a nod to the car's more technical, turbocharged spirit. The Classic Turbo's capsule wardrobe goes a step further, adding a 40mm Tambour Automatic watch in ceramic and yellow gold — chronometer-certified, powered by a rose gold micro-rotor, with 50 hours of power reserve and an invisible folding clasp that lets the bracelet wrap the wrist without interruption. A Full Wardrobe for Two Cars Naturally, neither car arrives without a matching capsule collection — because if you're commissioning a Louis Vuitton Porsche, you're not driving it in whatever you happen to be wearing. The Classic comes with a leather jacket detailed in Monogram Flower eyelets, a carbon-fiber helmet, and a made-to-measure three-piece luggage set with a roof rack built for a surfboard or skis. The Classic Turbo's capsule leans quieter and more tailored: a parachute-silk suit, driving gloves, and a Coffret Trésor — a case design first made by Louis Vuitton in 1896 — reimagined here to hold both the wristwatch and the dashboard clock when they're not in use. How Much Does It Cost to Drive a Piece of Watchmaking History? Neither Louis Vuitton nor Singer has disclosed pricing, and don't expect them to. Singer restorations typically start around $500,000 before any customization — and a project of this scope, layering in Swiss watchmaking and hand-finished leatherwork, will land well above that. If you have to ask, as they say. Both cars are one-of-a-kind. Which is, in the end, the whole point.

title: Panerai Clads the Luminor Marina in Carbotech
description: The new Panerai Luminor Marina PAM01707 pairs high-tech performance with a particularly refined interpretation of the brand’s historic design codes.
content: Panerai Clads the Luminor Marina in Carbotech A lightweight case meets a vintage-inspired icon Heritage Meets Cutting-Edge With the new Luminor Marina PAM01707, Panerai brings together two defining sides of its identity. On one hand, there is the unmistakable Luminor design, with its cushion-shaped case, prominent crown-protecting bridge and highly legible sandwich dial—features deeply rooted in the brand’s history as a supplier of precision instruments to the Italian Navy. On the other, Panerai turns to an advanced composite material that reduces weight, resists corrosion and gives every watch its own distinctive surface pattern. Naturally, the Luminor Marina PAM01707 is water-resistant to 300 meters, or 30 bar, and equipped with a manufacture movement with a power reserve of three days. An Individual Character At 44mm, the Luminor Marina PAM01707 retains the commanding proportions that have defined the collection for decades. Its case and bezel are crafted from Panerai's Carbotech, a composite material made by compressing layers of carbon fiber together with PEEK, a high-performance polymer that reinforces the material and contributes to its durability. The result is a lightweight yet highly resistant case with a distinctive matte-black surface. Because the layered material is cut differently for every case, the pattern varies from watch to watch, giving each PAM01707 an individual appearance. According to Panerai, Carbotech is 64 percent lighter than titanium and 80 percent lighter than steel while offering high resistance to corrosion— an advantage for a watch designed with underwater use in mind. Despite its 44mm diameter and 14.5 mm height, the watch weighs approximately 100 grams. A Familiar Design with a Softer Edge The matte black sandwich dial introduces a warmer and more restrained side to the Luminor’s traditionally instrumental design. Its large Arabic numerals and hour markers are filled with beige Super-LumiNova, which emits a green glow in the dark. The color combination recalls earlier Panerai tool watches while creating a softer contrast against the black dial and Carbotech case. The small seconds display at 9 o’clock is another reference to Panerai’s historic military watches. Originally, the running seconds hand allowed naval commandos to verify immediately that their watch was operating, even under difficult conditions. On the PAM01707, the date display has been omitted, resulting in a particularly clean and balanced dial layout that places the focus on the essential time indications. Three Days of Power Behind the closed titanium case back, the automatic P.9010 caliber ensures high precision. Equipped with two barrels connected in series, the manufacture movement provides a power reserve of three days. It also features a stop-seconds mechanism for precise time setting. When the crown is pulled out, the seconds hand stops, allowing the watch to be synchronized accurately. This function reflects Panerai’s military heritage, where exact time coordination was essential during naval operations. A quick-adjustment mechanism also allows the hour hand to be moved forward or backward in one-hour increments without affecting the minute hand or stopping the movement. This makes the PAM01707 particularly practical when traveling across time zones. A balance bridge secured on both sides contributes to the stability of the regulating organ, while four gold screws on the balance wheel allow its inertia to be precisely adjusted. Vintage Leather and Sporty Rubber Panerai supplies the watch with a warm brown calf leather strap and a black rubber strap. The interchangeable options allow the Luminor Marina to shift from a refined everyday watch with a strong heritage character to a more functional companion for water sports and active use. Pricing is marked at $15,600.

title: A Guide to Shinola's Updated Detrola Collection
description: The Motor City based brand introduces four new additions to its Detrola lineup, including limited-production Color Theory models inspired by contemporary art and, for the first time, core Detrola references fitted with metal bracelets.
content: A Guide to Shinola's Updated Detrola Collection Bold color meets everyday Detroit design Born and Raised in Detroit Since its founding in 2011, Shinola has positioned itself as a champion of American manufacturing and design, assembling watches in Detroit while drawing inspiration from the city’s rich industrial heritage and creative energy. The brand’s philosophy centers on creating well-designed everyday products that blend accessibility, craftsmanship, and distinctive aesthetics. Its Detrola collection, introduced as a colorful and lightweight alternative to the company’s steel-cased Runwell models, embodies that approach particularly well. Now Shinola is expanding the Detrola family with four new references that introduce fresh dial treatments, new bracelet options, and a display case back for the first time in the collection. Art-Inspired Color Theory Editions The most expressive additions are the limited-production Detrola Color Theory Cool and Detrola Color Theory Warm models. Both watches feature semi-matte 3D-printed dials inspired by abstract art and color studies, transforming the Detrola into a wearable canvas. The Theory Cool presents a playful composition of blue, pink, and mint-green tones. A field of geometric triangles appears to float across the dial, creating depth and movement while emphasizing the artistic concept behind the design. Printed mint-green minute tracking, warm gray hands filled with C1 Super-LumiNova, and a mint-green central seconds hand complete the vibrant display. Its counterpart, the Color Theory Warm, applies the same concept through a palette of orange and complementary hues, resulting in a more energetic visual character. Both watches feature a 41mm case consisting of a stainless-steel core co-molded with polished cream-colored TR90 resin. Additional design details include wire lugs, Shinola’s signature onion-shaped crown, sapphire crystal, and quick-release rubber straps matching the respective dial colors. For the first time within this series, a clear resin caseback allows a view of the movement inside. Detrola Goes Metallic Alongside the art-inspired editions, Shinola is introducing two permanent Detrola models that bring a more refined appearance to the collection. Most notably, they mark the first time that core Detrola references are available on a metal bracelet. The new Detrola Vapor Gold model features a warm gold-toned sunray dial paired with applied vertically brushed numerals and brushed silver hands with C1 Superluminova. The dial’s subtle metallic sheen contrasts with the transparent polished TR90 case, while a newly developed brushed silver brick-link bracelet gives the watch a cool presence on the wrist. The Cypress Green version follows the same formula but swaps the gold dial for a deep green sunray finish. Matte alabaster numerals, brushed silver hands, and an alabaster-colored seconds hand create a softer, more understated look. Like the Color Theory editions, both models measure 41mm in diameter, feature a stainless-steel case surrounded and sapphire crystals. They are also powered by the Argonite 705 quartz movement and proudly assembled in Detroit. Pricing is marked at $595.

title: Current Day Excellence: Walking Through Glashütte, Part III
description: Glashütte’s history is marked by hardship, but today the village stands as the heart of German watchmaking. “Made in Glashütte” is a seal of quality, yet its brands span a wide range of styles, uniting past, present, and future with unmistakable German character.
content: Current Day Excellence: Walking Through Glashütte, Part III A history of watchmaking in Glashütte As Glashütte still lacks a hotel, it is best to stay in Dresden when you want to explore the village. While Allied bombing raids leveled the entire historic center of this once-royal city during World War II, it has been rebuilt with dedication and precision. The city center is charming, and staying there also allows you to visit the Neues Grünes Gewölbe (New Green Vault). In this remarkable museum, you can admire the famous Dresden Green Diamond, among other treasures. Another must-visit is the Semperoper, a spectacular opera house that also houses the famous “Five-Minute Clock,” which inspired A. Lange & Söhne to create its signature outsize date. Staying in Dresden does mean that you have to drive into Glashütte, but that gives you the opportunity to travel through some of the most beautiful landscapes Germany has to offer. This tranquility is also an important ingredient for the watches made in Glashütte, as it greatly benefits the state of mind and sets the perfect scene for creating something as precise as a mechanical watch. The German Watch Museum is the ideal starting point for a visit to Glashütte. By recounting the village’s rich history, it sets the stage for everything that follows. Walking along the Hauptstrasse, “Main Street” in German, toward Ferdinand Adolph Lange Platz, we pass the old manufacture of A. Lange & Söhne, which has been restored to its former glory. While it is now mainly an administrative building, newer additional facilities nearby continue to produce A. Lange & Söhne watches largely by hand. This includes models launched at the brand’s rebirth in 1994 as well as newer creations such as the renowned Zeitwerk. Certain collections even have dedicated workshops. Engravings—most notably those on Lange balance cocks—are executed in specialized ateliers. In a remarkably short period of time, A. Lange & Söhne has become an industry benchmark, and the same can be said of its neighbor across the street. Nomos is located in Glashütte’s historic train station, one of several buildings the brand operates throughout town. Nomos is among the success stories born after the fall of the Berlin Wall opened new opportunities. Founded in 1990, the brand initially relied on outsourced movements but quickly evolved into a true manufacture. It has found a sweet spot—sufficient volume to satisfy demand and keep prices accessible, yet exclusive enough to remain firmly rooted in Glashütte tradition. Production blends high-tech machinery with significant manual labor. The only thing Nomos does not create in Glashütte is its design work, which is handled by Berlinerblau, the brand’s in-house creative agency in Berlin. From the classic Ludwig to the casual Club, the sporty Ahoi, and the luxurious Lambda, each model carries a clearly defined identity. Tutima is also housed in a former railway building, specifically Glashütte’s old rail maintenance depot. Beautifully restored like many historic structures in town, it operates in parallel with Tutima’s manufacture in Ganderkesee, where the brand functioned during the Cold War. With a rich aviation heritage, many Tutima models draw inspiration from flight instruments, notably the Flieger and Grand Flieger collections. Yet the brand also offers a refined side through collections such as Patria and Tempostopp, celebrating haute horlogerie at its finest. A standout example is the Hommage minute repeater. This duality—tool watches alongside high complications—is common in Glashütte, where brands often balance utilitarian roots with horological ambition. Across from the bus station between Nomos and Tutima stands the modern building of Glashütte Original, its large windows revealing a contemporary façade behind which traditional craftsmanship thrives. The company is the successor to Glashütter Uhrenbetrieb GmbH (GUB), founded in 1951 when the East German government merged most local watchmakers into a single entity. Despite challenging circumstances, innovation persisted. Today, Glashütte Original resurrects historic designs through its Vintage collection, including the Sixties and Seventies lines, while the SeaQ diver traces its lineage to historic predecessors. With the Senator and Pano collections, the brand also competes at the highest levels of watchmaking, pairing refined aesthetics with compelling complications. Union Glashütte is a sister brand to Glashütte Original under the Swatch Group umbrella. Founded more than 130 years ago by Johannes Dürrstein, Union developed a reputation for precision marine chronometers. After enduring the hardships of two world wars, the brand was revived in 1996. While initially integrated with Glashütte Original, it now operates independently and draws inspiration from vintage motorsport, evident in its sporty chronograph-heavy collection. Watchmaking is very much a family affair at Nautische Instrumente Mühle-Glashütte, where the sixth generation is preparing to take over. As the name suggests, the brand has deep ties to the nautical world, producing watches designed to withstand harsh maritime conditions. The S.A.R. Mission Time, developed for sea rescue operations, is emblematic of this philosophy. The collection also includes sport-oriented models in the Sportivo range and more refined offerings in the Teutonia and Lunova lines. Mühle-Glashütte remains a premium supplier of nautical instruments, including an extensive range of marine chronometers. Bruno Söhnle is another family-run brand that balances quality and value. Founded in 2000 by serial entrepreneur Bruno Söhnle as a 60th birthday gift to himself, the company is now led by his daughter Jennifer. Its headquarters occupy the former home of Julius Assmann, one of Glashütte’s founding watchmakers. The brand sources movements from suppliers such as ETA and Ronda, often reworking them extensively. Even quartz movements are decorated with traditional finishing, reflecting the brand’s belief in offering substance both inside and out. Moritz Grossmann remains one of the most esteemed names in Glashütte history. Today, the brand operates a manufacture overlooking the village and continues to produce watches largely by hand. Its designs are elegant and understated, emphasizing refined details and beautifully constructed movements. While precious metals dominate the collection, Moritz Grossmann has also embraced stainless steel, allowing for more sporty creations such as the Universalzeit, which displays seven time zones simultaneously through an ingenious dial system. Flip the watch over, and a traditional hand-wound movement reveals the brand’s uncompromising craftsmanship. Wempe is best known as Germany’s premier jeweler and watch retailer, but it has also been producing timepieces of its own for many years—naturally in Glashütte. The company restored the town’s historic observatory and transformed it into the home of Wempe Glashütte i/SA. This facility produces watches such as the Chronometerwerke, Iron Walker, and Zeitmeister, as well as nautical instruments. In collaboration with German state authorities, Wempe established the only chronometer certification center in Germany, adding yet another unique layer to Glashütte’s horological identity. All of this reinforces the magic of this small, almost hidden village. Decades of resilience, craftsmanship, and determination have made Glashütte the beating heart of German watchmaking—where history is not only preserved but actively lived every day.
